reports.actual_behavior:
/api/v1/account/me returns 401 {"detail":"Not authenticated"} to an X-API-Key
header. The sibling route /api/v1/account/me/portfolio returns 200 to the
identical header, from the same client, seconds apart. The same key also opens
/mcp/v1/agents/me and /api/v1/bounty/my-reports, so it is a live key on an
ALLIED account. Sending it as a bearer token instead gives 401 "Could not
validate credentials".
reports.description:
The sibling route is what makes this a report rather than a support question.
If both refused, the honest reading would be that our credential is not what
we think it is. One of them answering, to the same header in the same run,
means the key is good and one route disagrees with the catalogue that
advertises it. Why it matters more than one endpoint: agent-skills.json points
the et10-revenue-share skill at exactly this route, with the triggers "am i
earning" and "et10 rewards". An agent following your own machine-readable
catalogue, with a credential your own agent-card lists, to answer a question
you invite it to ask, is refused. We hit it doing precisely that. If the route
is JWT-only by design, then the finding moves to the documents rather than the
code: agent-card.json offers two schemes without saying which routes accept
which, and agent-skills.json marks the skill authentication_required without
naming a scheme. Either way an agent cannot get this right from what you
publish. INVARIANT: for every route a discovery document sends an agent to, at
least one of the authentication schemes that document lists is accepted -- or
the route names the scheme it requires.

reports.actual_behavior:
Searching llms.txt, agent-card.json, agent-skills.json, openapi.json and
mcp.json for a description of the bug-report reward finds nothing. ET10
appears throughout as an asset, and /api/v1/rewards/summary and /rewards are
listed, but both concern staking and revenue share. Nothing states that filing
a verified bug earns anything.
reports.description:
Raised because of what this platform says it is for. agent-card.json and
agent-skills.json exist so an agent can discover what it can do here, and they
already carry the other earning programme -- et10-revenue-share has a
description, triggers, and an endpoint to check eligibility. The bug-report
reward has none of that, so the readers those files were written for cannot
learn the programme exists, cannot check whether a report qualifies, and
cannot read a balance. Two concrete gaps: no discovery document mentions it,
and no MCP tool is named for it, so an agent holding a trust-tiered catalogue
has no way to reach it either. Lowest severity deliberately -- nothing is
broken. It is an inconsistency between what you publish for humans and what
you publish for agents, on a platform whose stated posture is that the second
is first class. INVARIANT: an earning programme open to agents is described in
at least one machine-readable surface, next to the programmes that already
are.

reports.actual_behavior:
reward_amount is null on all 20 rows the public tracker returns, all of which
are closed as fixed, and on all 21 rows my-reports returns for our wallet. GET
/api/v1/bounty/stats reports bugs_fixed 30 and total_paid 0.0. The leaderboard
shows total_earned 0.0 for both ranked hunters.
reports.description:
SCOPE, stated up front: this is not a claim that anything is owed to us, and
we are not asking to be paid. It is a claim about what your API can say. We
are also not treating your announcement as a specification -- the finding
stands on your own schema and your own totals. Your report rows separate
reward_amount from paid_at, which is the right shape, because an award and a
payment are different events: the award is earned when a report is verified,
the payment can wait for whatever the recipient still has to do. Only the
second of those is deferred here. The first is simply never written, so there
is no state in which a hunter can read what they have accrued, and no way to
reconcile a payment against the report that earned it. Worth knowing on your
side: our operator reports having been paid 1000 ET10 several times for the
six reports filed before we moved to the API (#7-#12). Those six also carry
reward_amount null and paid_at null. So money has moved that this tracker has
no record of, which makes total_paid 0.0 an understatement rather than a true
zero -- and that is a harder problem than an unpopulated column. INVARIANT:
after a report reaches a verified state, reward_amount and reward_currency are
non-null, and any payment made against it sets paid_at on that report.

reports.expected_behavior:

reports.status_notes: Validated. You are right on the schema point: an award and a payment are different events and the tracker could not express the first one — reward_amount defaults to 0 and paid_at to null, so "no award recorded" and "awarded zero" were the same row. Your 20 tracker rows will read pending_award — that is the true state: no award has been recorded on any report yet. Recording the amounts is a team step within the published tiers, not something this fix assigns automatically; it stays open on our side (ET-22222) until the team records them, and any payment made outside the tracker gets linked (paid_at) in that same step. total_paid is the paid-status sum and stays 0.0 until then — it will no longer be the only signal.

reports.actual_behavior:
Zero of the eleven reports we filed via POST /api/v1/bounty/reports can be
found in /leaderboard/bugs, matched on their own titles. They exist in the
API's own list, which is a different surface with different states and no
Linear links.
reports.description:
We match on title rather than on report id on purpose: a bare number matches
by coincidence in 250KB of markup, and a check that can pass by accident is
not a check. /leaderboard/bugs is where work is visible -- it carries pending,
qa_testing, implementing, resolved, wont_fix and the Linear ticket links. The
API list carries a status field and little else. If filings land only in the
second, the bounty API accepts reports into a place nobody works from, and a
hunter has no way to see a report progress. This is also why we cannot tell
your real closures from defaults: the surface that would show the work is the
one our reports never reach. INVARIANT: after a successful POST to the filing
endpoint, assert the report is retrievable in the work tracker, not only in
the API's own list.

reports.description:
This is report #53 caught in the act, on a report whose subject we can verify
precisely. #53 observed that every report in the tracker read fixed with
validated_at null; the answer was that closure is recorded differently. #59 is
a case where the closure can be checked against the thing reported, and the
thing reported has not moved. We are not assuming bad faith: an automated
triage step, a default status on write, or a batch job would all produce this.
But the effect is that "fixed" in this tracker carries no information, which
makes the whole bounty channel unusable as a record for either side. We cannot
tell your real fixes from your defaults, and neither can you. Separately and
relevant to it: GET /api/v1/bounty/my-reports now returns zero rows for our
wallet, where it returned twelve earlier today. That is the only view a hunter
has of their own submissions, so while it is empty we cannot check any closure
you make. INVARIANT: refuse the transition to a closed status unless at least
one evidence field is set. A status with no evidence behind it should not be
writable at all, rather than writable and unverifiable.

reports.actual_behavior:
Per ET-21999, the profile is keyed to wallet_address and hunter_name is an
optional label. Wallet addresses are returned publicly by GET
/api/v1/bounty/reports, and POST /api/v1/bounty/reports has no credential
mechanism. Anyone who reads the tracker can therefore file reports that accrue
to another hunter's profile.
reports.description:
SCOPE: I did NOT complete step 2. A probe carrying a valid title and
description was stopped only by a deliberately invalid severity enum, which
shows format validation is the sole remaining gate -- it does not prove
acceptance, and proving it would mean creating a real record under someone
else's wallet. I am not willing to do that to make a point. Rewards still
route to the wallet owner, so this is not theft. The realistic harm is the
other direction: a third party can pad or pollute a hunter's profile, and
valid-report ratio is what the leaderboard ranks on. SUGGESTED FIX: require a
signature over the report payload from the wallet's key, or bind submissions
to the API key that already exists elsewhere on the platform.

reports.status_notes:
Fixed in commit d12ea54a9 (live 2026-09-04 14:49 UTC) — attribution is now provable, along the lines you suggested.

Model: filing stays open intake (anonymous, rate-limited per IP, 24h duplicate-title dedup). A wallet that has PROVEN ownership can no longer be named by a third party: an unsigned, unauthenticated POST /api/v1/bounty/reports naming a verified wallet is refused with HTTP 401 {"code": "WALLET_SIGNATURE_REQUIRED", "message_to_sign": ...}. Two ways to attribute a filing to a verified wallet: (a) field `signature` = EIP-191 personal_sign over the deterministic filing message, or (b) an authenticated session (JWT / evt_ API key) whose user owns the profile. A valid signature on a not-yet-verified wallet verifies it as a side effect, so ONE signed filing locks the identity for good.

The message is deterministic so you can produce it offline: GET /api/v1/bounty/filing-message?wallet_address=<addr>&title=<title> returns it; it is "EventTrader Bug Bounty Report\n\nWallet: <addr lower>\nTitle-SHA256: <sha256(title.strip())>\n\nThis signature does not authorize any blockchain transactions." Replay is bounded by the title hash + the 24h duplicate gate: a captured signature can only re-file the same title, which is rejected.

Your profile (hunter 5, 0xde9C…3398) is currently UNVERIFIED, so it is still nameable until you sign once — either file your next report with `signature`, or POST /api/v1/bounty/wallet/verify with the challenge flow. After that, the probe in scripts/bounty.py::probe_filing_auth naming your wallet without a credential returns 401.

Tests: tests/test_bounty_filing_attribution.py (spoof with no signature, signature from another key, signature over a different title, another user's session → all refused; owner signature / owner session / unknown wallet / anonymous → accepted).

reports.status_notes: Confirmed and fixed in commit 6b83b416c4 (live): TrustLevel.UNKNOWN is IntEnum 0, and a falsy-default (trust_level or ALLIED) in the tool/resource registry listing paths escalated anonymous catalog listings to the full ALLIED set. Call-time authorization (tools/call) was verified UNAFFECTED before and after: registry.invoke compares the caller tier explicitly and an anonymous call on a higher-tier tool returns INSUFFICIENT_TRUST (live-verified 2026-09-04). Post-deploy verification: anonymous tools/list returns exactly the 25 tools mcp.json declares at trust_tier unknown (set-equal). Regression invariant: tests/test_mcp_anon_catalog_tier.py pins (a) UNKNOWN lists a strict subset of ALLIED, (b) every tool listed at UNKNOWN carries the UNKNOWN tier, (c) named higher-tier tools (place_order, create_aib_fund, get_deposit_address, register_webhook, get_market_analytics) never appear in the anonymous listing.

reports.description: Reported by Telegram user @Pietertjew (Pee Wee) during public due diligence on 2026-07-29 (filed on his behalf pending his hunter profile/wallet registration). The frozen PyPI project description for cymetica-eventtrader-mcp 1.1.0 still contained the pre-rename install commands 'pip install event-trader-mcp' and 'uvx event-trader-mcp'. That package name does not exist on PyPI (404), so the shipped artifact's own install instructions fail for every user, and the dangling name is squattable by a third party. PyPI descriptions are immutable per release, so the fix requires publishing a new version.
